title: Reproductive ecology of gulf toadfish (Opsanus beta)

authors.affiliation: University of West Florida, Florida USA
University of West Florida, Florida USA

abstract_text: Gulf toadfish, Opsanus beta, are poorly represented in ecological studies and their reproductive strategies relatively undefined. Our preliminary investigations into breeding seasons and mating behaviors of a Florida gulf toadfish population have revealed several unique and previously undocumented strategies. Ten replicates, each with 5 nest types, were placed in the field and observed from February until November for toadfish activities. Gulf toadfish appear to participate in a bi-peaked breeding season. Males established nests and females oviposit during the month of May, then all fish disappear until late July and breeding resumed in September. Male and female toadfish apparently discriminate between nest types differently. Females preferred nests with one opening over those that are accessible to the surrounding environment through multiple openings. Males, however, showed distinct preferences between the five different nest types based on characteristics of each nest. Males that occupy nests adjacent to other male-occupied nests appear to have greater reproductive success than lone males, contradicting the traditional view that toadfish are highly aggressive and territorial. Male gulf toadfish do not appear to aggressively defend any territory beyond their immediate nest site, an observation which may explain why males in groups experience greater reproductive success.

title: Reproduction of Pseudoplatistoma corruscans (Siluriformes: Pimelodidae) in the Parana River, State of Sao Paulo, Brazil

authors.affiliation: Departamento de Educacao, UNESP Campus de Assis, SP, Brazil

abstract_text: Pseudoplatistoma corruscans is a migratory species of economic interest. It is widely distributed in South America (in the basins of the Parana, San Francisco and Paraguay Rivers) and reproduces in floodplain lagoons where it spends the first phases of its life. Monthly collections, from January 1985 to January 1988, were performed in 150 km of Parana River, State of Sao Paulo, Brazil. A total of 255 fish were examined (56% young and 44% adults) measuring between 20.0 and 170.0 cm in total length. Data on body length at first sexual maturation was estimated to be 73.0 cm. This is larger than minimum capture size for this specie determined by the Brazilian Environmental Agency regulating fishing. The reproductive period coincided with the flood period from October to January and schools of mature fish were followed as far as Rio Pardo, a tributary of the Parana River. In the next months P. corruscans larvae were always collected in marginal ponds. These periodic floods promote the contact of the Parana River with the marginal ponds and are a requirement to the maintenance of the reproductive processes of P. corruscans.

title: Spatial and temporal patterns of reproductive and trophic divergence in bluegill sunfish

abstract_text: A study of bluegill populations from 12 Wisconsin lakes revealed significant differences among lakes in the degree of trophic specialization and sexual dimorphism. Morphological and behavioral variation within and among populations suggested that males compete most intensely for nesting sites in lakes with limited breeding area. Subsequent studies discovered additional bluegill colonies located in deeper areas of lakes for 4 of the most sexually-selected populations. Comparisons between deep-spawning and shallow-spawning colonies showed that deep-spawning bluegill possessed a trophic morphology typical of limnetic specialists and were less sexually dimorphic than bluegill from shallow colonies. Deep- and shallow-spawning bluegill did not differ in mean size or age, however there was greater variation in both age and size among males from the shallow colonies. The relative abundance of cuckolder males was significantly higher in shallow colonies. The mean number of eggs per nest did not differ between colony types, but variation in the number of eggs spawned per nest was greater in the shallow colonies. These data are consistent with the hypothesis that the intensity of sexual selection is greater in the shallow colonies, and that the deep colonies reflect an evolutionary alternative.

title: Morphology and life history of the marine threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus)

abstract_text: At the close of the last glacial period, only some 15,000 years ago, numerous and varied freshwater aquatic habitats were formed. The threespine stickleback was one of the first fish to colonize these habitats, and these populations have undergone a spectacular adaptive radiation. The threespine stickleback inhabiting nearby coastal marine habitats is the stock from which these freshwater populations were founded. Thus, both the direction and degree of change following freshwater isolation can be inferred by comparing freshwater and marine stickleback. However, the marine form actually may comprise two types: one living and breeding only in marine waters; and a second, anadromous type. At present we know relatively little about whether these types differ in any substantive way. Further, we know little about variation within these types. I present preliminary morphological and life-historical data showing that these types may not be as similar as previously thought, and I compare the level of apparent phenotypic variability with that exhibited by freshwater populations.

title: Evaluating the relationship between organismal trait values and body size, with an example from life-history data for the threespine stickleback, Gasterosteus aculeatus

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Clark University, Worcester, Massachusetts 01610, USA

abstract_text: The form of the relationship between values for organismal traits (e.g. clutch size) and organism body size has been of interest to biologists for >150 years. This interest has two, somewhat independent foci: to estimate the slope of the relationship itself, and to estimate size-free trait values for comparison across groups. Despite this long interest, there remains considerable controversy over the appropriate statistical model to use in each instance. Most studies use ordinary least squares regression for both, but this is only appropriate when the correlation between the trait of interest and size is quite high (i.e., > 0.9). Such high correlations are infrequent in life-history data sets. Presently, two alternatives for slope estimation appear to be gaining support: major axis regression, and reduced major axis regression. I apply all three methods to a data set for 50 threespine stickleback populations in order to illustrate the considerably different conclusions that can be generated for slopes. Size-adjustment is only appropriately performed using ordinary least squares procedures. Nevertheless, I use a subset of populations to illustrate how faulty conclusions can be generated here, also. No present statistical resolution to this latter problem is apparently in view.

title: Inter- and intra-latitudinal variation in life history traits in migrating silver-phase American eels, Anguilla rostrata

abstract_text: Migrating silver phase American eels were collected from two geographically separated pairs of rivers in Maine. title: Phenotypic plasticity in life history traits of Gambusia puncticulata puncticulata (Poeciliidae) from the Cayman Islands, BWI

abstract_text: Gambusia p. puncticulata is a common resident of saline ponds which show high spatio-temporal variability in physico-chemical conditions. Plasticity in life-history traits of these populations may be tied to the dynamic nature of their environment.

title: Ethnoichthyology of Piracicaba River fishermen (Southeastern Brazil)

authors.affiliation: Nucleo de Estudos e Pesquisas Ambientais, Universidade Estadual de Campinas, Campinas, SP, Brazil

abstract_text: Ethnoichthyology is the part of science that studies the relationships between people and fish, including folk knowledge. Fishermen usually have knowledge on fish biology and behavior, which is often useful to ichthyologists. We conducted an ethnoichthyological study with fishermen from the impounded portion of the Piracicaba River (Southeastern Brazil), interviewing 22 fishermen (17 men and 5 women) using questionnaires based on pictures of ten fish species. We showed the pictures at random, in the same order for all people interviewed. Fishermen showed a detailed knowledge about diet, predators, spatial and temporal distributions, reproduction and migratory patterns. Many information provided by fishermen fitted well with the biological observations from the scientific literature. Fishermen exhibit a great knowledge on diet, predators, migratory movements and habitat requirements of fishes. This could be due to the constant observation of these phenomenons by fishermen and due to the importance of this information to the fishery. Fishermen known more about common and commercially valuable fish species, and known less about rare species. The value and abundance of the fishes, the usefulness in the fishery, as well the frequent observation of the biological attributes of abundant species are important factors influencing the Piracicaba River fishermen knowledge about fish.

abstract_text: Supernumerary, or B, chromosomes are morphologically distinct chromosomal elements that are found in addition to the normal chromosome complement. They may show numerical variation within and between individuals and are highly variable in their effect, morphology, and inheritance pattern. These chromosomes, thought to arise either from the autosomal chromosome set or through interspecific hybridization, appear to evolve independently of the normal chromosome set. Supernumerary chromosomes are present in the Pacific giant salamander, Dicamptodon tenebrosus. Individuals of this species that we examined possessed up to 8 supernumeraries, with population means ranging from 0.5 to 2.67 per individual. Supernumerary chromosomes from two D. tenebrosus individuals were microdissected, cloned and partially sequenced to analyze their genetic make-up. We used these DNA segments as probes for use in Southern blots to determine whether or not homologies exist between supernumerary chromosomes and the normal chromosome set. The DNA composition of these supernumerary chromosomes and their origin and evolution in D. tenebrosus will be discussed.

abstract_text: The H. viridiflavus complex is considered to comprise a number of sub-species, based on dorsal colouration patterns. abstract_text: The Neotropical genus Hemiphractus comprises 5 species. Frogs in this genus have long been assumed to represent a natural group of species. Previous work by us corroborated the monophyly of Hemiphractus and placed it within the genus Gastrotheca — i.e., Gastrotheca is paraphyletic with respect to Hemiphractus. title: Testing of amphibian dispersal scenarios with hypervariable DNA

abstract_text: In pond-breeding amphibian species, dispersal between demes reduces the chance for local extinction. abstract_text: The phylogenetic relationships among tropical taxa are poorly known when compared to temperate counterparts. abstract_text: Six taxa of crested and marbled newts (subgenus Triturus) have largely parapatric distributions across Europe, with or without hybridization taking place between them. abstract_text: The Banggai cardinalfish, Pterapogon kauderni Koumans 1933 has been the focus of the pet trade since its "rediscovery" a few years ago. abstract_text: Moxostoma spawning acts involve one female and two or more males, and occur by intense quivering into gravel and/or cobble. In trio spawning the female is symmetrically held and pressed laterally to dorsolaterally during oviposition. In the more derived species, the two adjacent nest-holding (Dear Enemy) males repel intruders that perturb or dispel the female from spawning. It takes two males to tango, perhaps best so in suckers.

abstract_text: Declines in populations of some formerly common, widespread amphibians and reptiles in Idaho indicate the need for a statewide monitoring program. abstract_text: Caecilians are circumtropically distributed amphibians exhibiting many adaptations to a fossorial existence including limblessness, reduced eyes and a strongly ossified skull. title: Are calling surveys the best method to use to monitor all frogs?

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Black Hills State University, USB #9044, Spearfish, SD 57799-9044, USA

abstract_text: Concerns over population declines and reports of malformations have led many agencies to become interested in inventory and monitoring of amphibians, especially frogs. Most of these programs rely primarily on calling surveys. Volunteers are often used in these efforts, and they are not necessarily trained herpetologists. For two years, my survey teams have conducted surveys of several species in a variety of habitats in western South Dakota. We have found that calling surveys are not necessarily the best census method for all anurans, and they may result in misleading conclusions. For federal lands in western South Dakota, we recommend calling surveys to monitor only one species, the chorus frog (Pseudacris triseriata). For most other species, calling surveys give misleading results or their success may depend on detailed knowledge of anuran life histories. Species which breed at temporary wetlands are easily overlooked when calling survey routes are designed. Calling behavior also appears to depend on certain climatic factors which have yet to be fully understood. Limited funds may be better spent on life history studies and on studies of chorusing behavior before calling surveys become favored as the primary method of inventory and monitoring of anurans across North America.

title: Testing for treatment effects using home range: a herpetologist's perspective

authors.affiliation: University of Guelph, Department of Zoology, Guelph, Ontario N1G 2W1

abstract_text: Home range analyses are commonly used by herpetologists to test aspects of behaviour, demographics, reproductive strategies, and other aspects of ecology. Unfortunately, herpetologists (and other ecologists) often do not use the same rigorous standards when analyzing home ranges that they use for other statistical procedures. Home ranges are frequently estimated using different sample sizes, time intervals among observations, and total sampling periods, either among animals or among treatments. Using simulations and radiotelemetry data from snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina), I demonstrate that home range estimates are dependent upon these three aspects of the sampling regime. In order to adequately test for treatment effects, home ranges must be analyzed using similar sample sizes and time intervals. Ironically, one aspect of home range analysis which ecologists have attempted to improve is autocorrelation. Traditionally, autocorrelation is believed to violate the assumptions of home range estimates, and so ecologists often subsample observations to reduce autocorrelation. However, I demonstrate that the accuracy and precision of home range estimates may improve with increasing autocorrelation, and reducing autocorrelation may cause more problems than it solves.

title: Home range analysis of the common musk turtle (Sternotherus odoratus) in fragmented habitat

abstract_text: We studied a population of common musk turtles (Sternotherus odoratus) in Georgian Bay, Ontario. Using radio-location data from the musk turtles we compared the accuracy of these three home range estimators. Cluster analysis was only more accurate than the harmonic mean estimator. However, the variability in accuracy was considerably less for cluster analysis relative to minimum convex polygon. We concluded that cluster analysis is a more appropriate home range estimator for animals in fragmented habitat than the minimum convex polygon or harmonic mean estimators.

title: The influence of body size and kinship on aggression and contest outcomes in hatchling snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina)

title: Spotted turtle (Clemmys guttata) hibernation near the northern range limit

abstract_text: Spotted turtles (Clemmys guttata) are listed as "Vulnerable" in Canada, and are similarly listed throughout the eastern U.S. Not much is known about hibernation in this species, therefore information on site fidelity and communal hibernaculum use may be important to the creation of conservation programs. Using temperature-sensitive radiotransmitters and miniature dataloggers, we monitored the phenology and temperatures at entrance into and exit from hibernation over 4 winters (1993-97). Nineteen hibernacula occupied by a total of 34 turtles were discovered; 12 hibernacula were apparently occupied by individual turtles and 7 were used communally (minimum of 2-6 individuals). title: Predation on Clemmys guttata and Chelydra serpentina nests in a dolomite prairie

title: A population study of painted turtles, Chrysemys picta: the effects of timing of nesting on nest temperatures and sex ratios

abstract_text: During the course of field work over a 10-year period with the arboreal boa Corallus grenadensis on the West Indian island of Grenada, locals (e.g., farmers, forestry officials) invariably informed us that tree boas were not as common as they had been in the past. We also explored whether shelter reuse contributes to population social structure. title: A quantitative comparison of fish communities from mangrove and seawall habitats in a southeastern United States estuarine system

title: Conservation of the bayou darter, Etheostoma rubrum (Percidae): larval ecology and population structure

title: Using surrogate species to develop endangered species recovery plans: Conceptual and methodological issues

title: The influence of the Dawesville Channel on the fish fauna of the shallows of the Peel-Harvey Estuary

title: Biology of the greater redhorse (Moxostoma valenciennesi) - a neglected species

abstract_text: Biology of the greater redhorse was studied in the middle reaches of the Grand River, Ontario from 1995 to 1997. Spawning began in late May when water temperatures were above 13°C, and lasted for up to 14 days. Spawning occurred in shallow riffle areas comprised of pebble, cobble and gravel. Videographic observations indicated that males usually remained on or near the spawning riffles and females were either attracted by the presence or conspicuous behaviour of males. Males produced rapid snout vibrations which usually preceded spawning activity. Post spawning movements and habitat use were determined using radio telemetry. After spawning, most fish moved several kilometres downstream and occupied deeper margins of riffles, usually in aggregation with conspecifics. By early summer, fish had dispersed evenly throughout the 17 km study reach. An access point creel survey indicated that there was a significant recreational fishery targeting greater redhorse, although anglers were unsure of the correct name for the species. Very little information is available on the greater redhorse, or any member of the Moxostomatini tribe, although it is an important and conspicuous species in the middle reaches of the Grand River, and likely elsewhere.

title: The role of artificial reefs in fisheries and ecosystem management

authors.affiliation: Florida Center for Environmental Studies, 135 NE 19th Ave., Cape Coral, Florida 33909 USA

abstract_text: Artificial reefs currently play only a minor role in fisheries or ecosystem management. The most notable example is their use in the spiny lobster fishery. Further examination of the role that artificial reefs can play in fisheries management needs to be explored. An example may be with regard to facilitating recruitment of juvenile and young adult serranid fishes (grouper and seabass) from inshore grassbeds to offshore, natural reefs. Further, artificial reefs can play a significant role in sanctuary and marine reserve programs. Moreover, purposeful and timed exploitation/rehabilitation of fish assemblages through artificial reefs may help sustain both fisheries and fish assemblages. Artificial reefs may not be effective in habitat mitigation where natural habitat has been destroyed. Information on the complete role that reefs play in trophic dynamics therefore needed. Additionally, an understanding of the time and spatial scales necessary to effect management objectives is essential. While, most artificial reef research, to date, has been directed toward fish and fish assemblages, additional insight into ecological processes and large scale ecosystem management may be gleaned through their study. In the future, artificial reefs construction and deployment design should be directed toward adding to our knowledge base to better manage nearshore and coastal ecosystems. Interagency, interstate, and international cooperation are the cornerstones for this endeavor. Both the positive and negative features of artificial reef deployment as a management tool need to be understood before they are generally accepted as a ecosystem management alternative.

title: Species at risk in the Gulf of Mexico and adjacent coastal habitats: a website

abstract_text: A website (http://www.ims.usm.edu/~musweb/endanger.html) has been created that provides information on vertebrate and invertebrate species potentially at risk in the Gulf of Mexico and adjoining coastal habitats. The website was developed as a means to disseminate the results of a workshop on the identification of potentially endangered species in the Gulf and to establish research needs for these species through a cooperative agreement between the US Gulf of Mexico Program and Gulf Coast Research Laboratory Museum. Detailed information is provided for 78 species, including 24 fish, 3 amphibians, and 8 reptiles. Data include synonyms, nomenclatural remarks, distinguishing features, similar species, species photographs, summaries of species biology, distribution, size, scientific basis for assessment of risk, status of gulf populations, and bibliographies. For fishes, online distributional maps and extensive archival records for each species were compiled through the assistance of many collections, most notably those of the five gulf states. These compilations were used to assess historical changes in species distributions. A bibliography of over 8,500 papers dealing with endangered species and related topics is also available, as well as links to other related websites. Extensions are directed toward more structured data collection, standardized online databasing, and inclusion of non-indigenous species so that information can readily accessed for management and educational purposes.

title: Fine structure of the notochord of the chestnut lamprey

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of Wisconsin Stevens Point, Stevens Point, WI 54481 USA
Department of Biology, University of Wisconsin Stevens Point, Stevens Point, WI 54481 USA

abstract_text: The notochord of the lamprey is a solid cylindrical organ consisting of a cellular medulla surrounded by an extracellular fibrous sheath and an elastic externa. The base of the medulla consists of a layer of columnar cells with an extensive network of rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. The cytoplasm of these cells also contains distinct lipid droplets and a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. The vacuoles in the cells located in the middle of the medulla are reinforced with a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. These cells are interconnected with numerous desmosomes. Lipid droplets and huge deposits of glycogen granules are also observed in the vacuolated cells. The fibrous sheath is made of several layers of collagen fibers. Interspersed between the collagen layers are deposits of extracellular matrix similar to that found in the elastic externa. The elastic externa is an amorphous layer of extracellular matrix that appears to be secreted by the fibroblasts and chondroblasts that surround the periphery of the notochord. There are several differences in the organization of the lamprey notochord when compared to the fine structure of the sturgeon and lungfish notochord (J. Morphol. 1998). These differences may have functional and phylogenetic implications that remain to be determined.

title: Osteology of the remora (Echeneididae: Carangoidei) sucking disc

authors.affiliation: Center for Biodiversity and Conservation Biology, Royal Ontario Museum, 100 Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario M5S 2C6, Canada; and Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1A1, Canada

abstract_text: Remoras (Echeneididae: Carangoidei) are medium sized, specialized pelagic fishes, inhabiting the warm water of the world. Remoras are found in close association with certain marine animals and inanimate objects. In all cases remoras use their sucking disc to attach to smooth surfaces. An osteological examination of cleared and stained remoras reveals that the disc is homologous with the dorsal fin of other percoids. The disc is composed of 4 structures: proximal, medial and distal pterygiophores, and the dorsal spines. These 4 structures are serially repeated to form the disc. The dorsal spine is reduced in size and enclosed in the fin membrane. The paired distal pterygiophore forms the denticulated laminae, and also supports the spine. The medial pterygiophore forms the perimeter of the disc, and supports the laminae forming a hinged joint which allows rotation. The proximal pterygiophore supports the entire unit, it connects to both the laminae and the medial pterygiophore. Each of these units is connected to the previous one by the proximal pterygiophore. The remora attaches itself by pressing the disc against a surface and rotating the distal pterygiophore around the hinged joint. This increases the volume of the sealed chamber creating a partial vacuum.

title: Development of the cartilaginous cephalic skeleton in the sole, Solea solea (Pleuronectiformes, Soleidae)

authors.affiliation: Universite de Liege, Institut de Zoologie, Laboratoire de Morphologie fonctionnelle et evolutive, 22 Quai Van Beneden, B-4020 Liege, Belgium

abstract_text: The postembryonic development of the cartilaginous cephalic skeleton in Solea solea (Linne) was observed from hatching to the juvenile stage. Fry were trypsin-cleared and alcian-blue stained. At hatching, S. solea displays no cartilaginous structure. On day 3, the fry exhibit trabecular bars, Meckel's cartilages, palatoquadrates, hyosymplectics, hyoid bars, the first two ceratobranchials and basibranchials 1-3. On day 4, ceratobranchials 3 and 4 form. On day 12, short taeniae marginales are formed on the well-developed otic capsules and the branchial basket is nearly complete. On day 14, cartilage reduction begins as the posterior part of the trabecula communis separates from the otic capsules. On day 18, metamorphosis begins. The tectum posterius completes posteriorly the braincase dome. On day 20, the left eye moves to the median crest of the head and the right eye shifts a bit downwards. Consequently, displacement of the right eye induces a deformation extending to the right pterygoid process. On day 23, both eyes are located on the same side. On day 29, cartilage reduction affects the hyosymplectics; it continues with the first two ceratobranchials on day 32 and with the otic capsules on day 40.

title: Volumetric study of brain regions in Xenopoecilius oophorus (Beloniformes: Adrianichthyidae)

authors.affiliation: Department of Anatomy, Nippon Medical School, Sendagi 1-1-5, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo 113 Japan

abstract_text: Xenopoecilius oophorus is a member of the basal clade of Adrianichthyidae. In order to determine the size and shape of brain regions in these fishes I used a 3-dimensional computer reconstruction system (TRI 3.10). To preserve the original size of structures specimens were immersion-fixed in 10% formalin and brains sectioned at 30 um on a cryostat. Outlines of 180 serial sections were traced to calculate the volume of one whole brain and six brain regions; olfactory bulbs (BO), telencephala (TE), optic tecta (TO), inferior lobes (IL), cerebellum (CE), and facial lobes (FL). Volumetric estimates from sampling every section were compared with estimates from sampling each 2nd, 4th and 8th section, as well as from ocular micrometry using linear measurements taken under a dissecting microscope. Estimates from section sampling and ocular micrometry did not differ significantly from the complete volumetric values. Estimates from ocular micrometry were derived from the ellipsoid model [V=1/6 pi*lwd] (l=length, w=width, and d=depth), except for the TO, which was estimated from [V=SA*T] (SA=surface area, T=thickness). Estimates of total brain size derived by measuring the linear distance between the anterior margin of the telencephalon and the obex did not differ significantly from estimates derived from weighing brains.

title: Pleomerism of vertebrae, fin rays, and scale rows in the gobiid fishes: observations and possible explanations

authors.affiliation: Severtsev Institute of Ecology and Evolution, Moscow 117071, Russia

abstract_text: According to Lindsey (1975), pleomerism is a correlation among related animal species between their numbers of meristic parts and their characteristic body sizes. Lindsey found a striking tendency for vertebral number to be positively correlated with maximum length in many families of fish; however, he did not find the same correlation among 36 species of the family Gobiidae in his analysis. Data on the maximum recorded size, numbers of vertebrae, fin-rays (in dorsal, anal, and pectoral fins), and scales in longitudinal row were taken from published reviews of the gobiid species occurring in the Indo-West-Pacific (120 species), South African (107), North East Atlantic (73), Black Sea (26) regions. Not only vertebral numbers, but all other counts appeared to be positively correlated with size of gobiid species in the four regions. Taxonomic applications of this phenomena and possible evolutionary explanations (e.g., life history correlates, structure of heritable morphological variation) are discussed.

title: Functional morphology of pectoral fin locomotion in basal actinopterygians

authors.affiliation: Department of Organismal Biology and Anatomy, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637 USA
Department of Zoology, Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago, IL 60605 USA

abstract_text: Fishes use their pectoral fins for a variety of locomotor functions including providing thrust for rectilinear movement. Most previous analyses of pectoral fin swimming in fishes have focused on the Perciformes, a relatively derived group. In this study we examine pectoral fin swimming in Polypterus palmas, Lepisosteus platostomus, and Amia calva, representing three basal clades of ray-finned fishes. Both forward and reverse swimming are analyzed to reflect the wide range of behaviors during which fishes use their pectoral fins. Anatomical changes which have occurred in the pectoral fin complex include duplication of musculature and the formation of a specialized fin ray to act as the leading edge of the fin. Kinematically, the frequencies of fin beats and three-dimensional excursions of the fin differ greatly between species. Electromyograms reveal differences in the duration, relative timing, and amplitude of activity in the pectoral muscles suggesting that motor patterns during swimming are not highly conserved in these taxa. These data are compared with information from more derived taxa to trace the evolution of pectoral fin swimming in actinopterygians.

title: Geographic variation in the skeleton of the stoneroller, Campostoma anomalum

authors.affiliation: Museum of Biological Diversity, The Ohio State University, 1315 Kinnear Road, Columbus, OH 43212 USA

abstract_text: Comparative osteology of the nominal species Campostoma anomalum was investigated across most of its geographic range in North America. Considerable variation was found associated with the food cropping and food processing mechanisms (jaws, pharyngeals) and bones associated with the operation of these structures. Transformations in character states (using Campostoma ornatum and Dionda diaboli as outgroups) were found in the jaws, pharyngeals, suspensorium, opercular series, sphenotic, ethmoid, cranial roof and vertebral number. Results from the skeletal analysis were interpreted as follows. Two broadly defined groups were recognized. One, represented by Campostoma anomalum pullum, is widespread across the glaciated mid-section of North America and southward in the plains region. The second is a complex of forms (represented in the upper Ohio Valley by Campostoma a. anomalum) distributed in the Ohio River basin and peripheral areas to the east, south and west. The stonerollers found in the northern portions of the Ohio Valley can be pullum, anomalum or possible intermediates between the two depending on the drainage system. The largescale stoneroller, C. 'oligolepid', distributed in the Ozark uplands is a western component of the anomalum complex that is related to the similar but slightly more derived Tennessee-Cumberland stoneroller. The stoneroller that dominates the Tennessee-Cumberland is the most derived form of the anomalum complex. It has peripheral (extensions?) in the Green River, New River and on the gulf and east slopes. The name C. a. michauxi Fowler might apply to this form. Two of the most recognizable populations within the anomalum complex have smaller distributional ranges. One is found in the Roanoke-James and the other in the Ouachita drainage.

title: Sperm competition and the evolution of alternative male life histories

authors.affiliation: University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5
University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5
University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5

abstract_text: Sperm competition is one vehicle by which males compete with each other for reproductive success. This paper examines sperm competition between the specialized cuckolder and parental male life histories of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). First, we find that the investment in total sperm production is higher in cuckolders than parentals and within cuckolders, males that have higher sperm production obtain higher fertilization success. Second, the longevity of sperm is lower in cuckolders than parentals. The alternative male reproductive life histories of bluegill therefore utilize sperm in different ways to compete for reproductive success. Cuckolders invest in quantity because they always face sperm competition, while parentals invest in quality because they only rarely face sperm competition. We compare these findings to those in other fishes by analyzing differences in sperm competition intensities and sperm quantity-quality tradeoffs.

title: Sturgeons and their parasites: the historical biogeography of a host-parasite association

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5
Department of Zoology, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg

abstract_text: Sturgeons (Osteichthyes: Acipenseridae) are evolutionary relicts with a wide distribution in the northern hemisphere. The historical biogeography of their association with their diverse assemblage of host specific parasites is explored using phylogenetic systematics and information from geology, paleontology and paleogeography. The patterns indicate historical exchanges with a variety of host taxa and low levels of conspeciation, resulting in small clades of widely distributed parasite species. Sister taxa of parasites generally exhibit allopatric patterns associated with discrete landmasses and basins. A trans-Atlantic track involving Acipenser oxyrhynchus and A. sturio and a trans-Pacific track involving A. medirostris are evident. The parasite relationships also support a historical connection between North America and North Asian freshwater sturgeons (A. fulvescens and A. baeri or their ancestors) and the biogeographical and phylogenetic relationship of A. fulvescens and A. brevirostrum. Based on these parascript studies, it is hypothesized that a former contiguous distribution of Palaeartic and Neartic sturgeons was fragmented by climatic and tectonic events in the Tertiary causing displacement of the lake sturgeon lineage and its association with the Gulf of Mexico drainages.

title: Biogeography of giant bacteria and their surgeonfish (Acanthuridae) hosts in the north Pacific

abstract_text: Surgeonfishes harbor a group of gut symbionts that include the largest known Eubacteria (cell lengths of 30 um to >500 um). Because the bacteria are acquired after larval surgeonfishes settle from the plankton, the fish/symbiont system in the Hawaiian Archipelago and other north Pacific locations provides an opportunity to address questions about evolution of host and symbionts within and among hosts, within and among islands, and among island systems. We have surveyed microbes in host surgeonfishes from Hawaii, Maui, Oahu, Kauai, French Frigate Shoals, Pearl & Hermes, and Midway Islands in the Hawaiian Archipelago, as well as from the Red Sea, Great Barrier Reef, Tuvalu, Moorea (French Polynesia), Ishigaki Island (Japan) and Gulf of California. A variety of structural morphs of the bacteria, differing in maximum size, cell shape, and the number and mode of formation of daughter cells, have been recorded from all sites except the Gulf. There appears to be considerable consistency in morphs occupying particular host species among the Hawaiian islands, but little consistency among island systems in terms of morphs occupying given host species. Preliminary molecular studies suggest local divergence of microbes within a single host, at least for widely separated localities.
